subject: radiology
title: Radiation Safety Principles: ALARA, Bio-Effects, and Dose Limits

steps.title: The ALARA Mandate and Cardinal Rules
steps.tx: **ALARA safety principle** mandates that all medical radiation exposures be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable, with economic and societal factors taken into account. Practical implementation relies on three cardinal safety tools: minimizing exposure time near radiation sources, maximizing physical distance utilizing the inverse square law, and deploying structural lead shielding barriers to attenuate transmitted scatter rays.

steps.title: Deterministic Tissue Reactions
steps.tx: **Deterministic radiation effects** occur following lethal cellular damage and exhibit a specific minimum dose threshold below which the clinical pathology does not develop. Above this threshold, the biological severity of the reaction increases proportionally with increasing dose. Classic examples include transient cutaneous erythema at 2 grays, temporary epilation at 3 grays, and radiation-induced ocular cataracts at 0.5 gray.

steps.title: Stochastic Carcinogenesis Mechanics
steps.tx: **Stochastic radiation risk** results from non-lethal, sublethal DNA mutations in reproductive or somatic stem cells. Under the internationally accepted linear no-threshold radiobiological model, there is no safe radiation threshold below which cancer cannot occur: every increment of exposure adds statistical probability. However, unlike deterministic injuries, the clinical severity of resulting radiation-induced cancer is entirely independent of the initiating dose.

left.title: Deterministic Effects
points: Direct cell killing; clear dose threshold exists
Severity of injury increases with increasing dose
Examples include skin burns, epilation, and cataracts

right.title: Stochastic Effects
points: Sublethal DNA mutations; no dose threshold exists
Probability increases with dose; severity is constant
Examples include radiation-induced leukaemia and solid tumours

steps.title: Occupational Whole-Body Dose Limits
steps.tx: **Occupational dose limits** are established by the International Commission on Radiological Protection and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board to prevent deterministic injuries and limit stochastic hazards. Radiation workers must not exceed an effective dose of 20 millisieverts per year averaged over five consecutive calendar years, with an absolute ceiling of 50 millisieverts in any single year.

rows: Averaged over 5 years (max 50 mSv in any 1 year)
Applies for the remainder of gestation
Excludes natural background and personal medical exams

steps.title: Organ-Specific Occupational Thresholds
steps.tx: **Equivalent organ limits** prevent deterministic reactions in highly exposed localized anatomical regions. The occupational equivalent dose limit for the lens of the eye was revised downward to 20 millisieverts per year averaged over five years, down from the historic 150 millisieverts, following evidence of radiation cataracts at lower thresholds. The annual equivalent limit for skin, hands, and feet remains 500 millisieverts.

left.title: Ocular Lens Limit
points: Mandated at 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years
Cannot exceed 50 mSv in any individual year
Requires lead acrylic eyewear during interventional cases

right.title: Extremities and Skin Limit
points: Mandated at 500 mSv per calendar year
Averaged over any 1 cm2 area of irradiated skin
Protects fluoroscopists handling hands near direct beam

steps.title: Public Radiation Exposure Ceilings
steps.tx: **Public dose limits** protect non-radiation workers and visitors in healthcare facilities. The statutory limit for members of the general public is 1 millisievert effective dose per year. In special circumstances, a higher dose may be permitted in a single year provided the five-year average remains under 1 millisievert annually. The equivalent public limit for the ocular lens is 15 millisieverts.

steps.title: Thermoluminescent Dosimeter Mechanics
steps.tx: **Thermoluminescent dosimeter badge** monitoring tracks cumulative occupational radiation over three-month service periods. Inside the badge, dysprosium-doped calcium sulphate crystals absorb incoming radiation, trapping excited electrons within metastable lattice defects. During laboratory processing, heating the card to 280 degrees Celsius releases trapped electrons back to ground states, emitting visible light whose intensity is proportional to absorbed dose.

steps.title: Dosimeter Badge Placement Protocols
steps.tx: **Dosimeter placement protocol** rules require diagnostic workers to wear a single TLD badge at chest level beneath their lead apron to measure whole-body effective dose. In high-exposure fluoroscopy and interventional radiology suites, a two-badge system is mandated: one badge is worn under the apron at chest height, while a second badge is worn outside the lead collar at the neck.
